title: Teaching on Purpose #13: Driving Hard Thinking
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: Adam Kohlbeck introduces the sixth of Chiltern Learning Trust's core teaching purposes—Driving Hard Thinking—through an interview with teacher Yamina Bibi. He distinguishes 'hard thinking' from 'difficult thinking,' defining it as sustained grappling with challenge at depth, often in service of application, that is not served by the other five core purposes. Kohlbeck emphasizes that students are inference-making machines whose connections to prior knowledge must be curated by teachers, since left to chance, wrong connections form. He frames thinking as needing to happen about the right thing, in the right way, and at the right time within a learning sequence. Socratic seminars are presented as a key technique for hard thinking, structured with inner and outer rings of students playing distinct roles. The post cautions that Socratic seminars are most effective when students have sufficient foundational knowledge, and should not be used when understanding is still emerging.
points: Hard thinking is defined as sustained grappling with challenge at depth in service of application—distinct from the attention, meaning-making, and recall that other teaching purposes address.

Kohlbeck's six core purposes—securing attention, communicating meaning, driving hard thinking, enabling practice, utilizing memory, and checking for understanding—frame every instructional decision at Chiltern Learning Trust.

Socratic seminars, with structured inner and outer student rings, are most powerful at the start or end of a unit when students have sufficient knowledge to synthesize and connect, not when understanding is still emerging.
quotes: Thinking is fundamental to learning. If memory is the reside of thought (Willingham, 2009) then as teachers, we have to be conscious of the extent to which we are helping students to think about the right thing, in the right way at the right time.

Students are inference making machines and with every new piece of knowledge or new experience they gain, comes a raft of potential connections to existing knowledge or experiences. Often, these connections aren’t the right ones!
When we say ‘Driving hard thinking’, we don’t mean ‘hard’ as in ‘difficult’. We also don’t mean to suggest that ‘hard thinking’ is the only type of thinking that students do.
Hard thinking – sustained grappling with challenge at depth and often in service of application is different. It isn’t served through the other purposes and so it is a purpose in its own right.

Socratic seminars are most useful at the start or end of a unit of work. At the start, they are an opportunity for students to process and verbalise what they already think and know about a topic. At the end, they are an opportunity for students to articulate what they have come to know and how they have come to think about the topic.

When student understanding is still emerging, it is likely that teachers would be best served curating the connections that students make with new or existing knowledge. If knowledge is still on the weaker end of the spectrum, they are unlikely to be able to use it to synthesise and connect and it is this opportunity that yields the benefit of Socratic seminars.
